label: def:high-dim-distribution
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:high-dim-distribution}
For a unit vector $u\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1}$ and a distribution $A$ on the real line with probability density function $A(\cdot)$, define $P^{A}_u$ to be the distribution over $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $P^{A}_u$ is the product distribution whose orthogonal projection onto the direction of $u$ is $A$, 
and onto the subspace perpendicular to $u$ is the standard $(d-1)$-dimensional normal distribution. 
That is, $P^{A}_u(x) = A(u^\top x) {\rm{exp}}\left(-\|x - (u^\top x)u\|_2^2/2\right)/(2\pi)^{(d-1)/2}$.

label: lm:hat-epsilon-guarantee
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm:hat-epsilon-guarantee}
	Suppose $P = P_{\epsilon, \theta, Q} $ for some $\epsilon \in [0, 0.05], \theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and some distribution $Q$. Suppose $\widehat{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ satisfies $\|\widehat{\theta} - \theta\| \leq 1$. For the $\widetilde{\epsilon}$ defined in \eqref{ineq:hat-epsilon}, we have 
    \[ \|\widehat{\theta}- \theta\| \leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{\log(1 /\widetilde{\epsilon} )} } \]
   for some universal constant $C>0$.

label: th:hat-epsilon-guarantee
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:hat-epsilon-guarantee}
Suppose $P=P_{\epsilon,\theta,Q}$
for some \(\epsilon\in[0,0.05]\), \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and some distribution \(Q\). Assume that \(\widehat{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfies
$\|\widehat{\theta}-\theta\|\le 1$.
Then the quantity \(\widetilde{\epsilon}\) defined in (\ref{ineq:hat-epsilon-relax}) satisfies
\[
\|\widehat{\theta}-\theta\|
\le
\frac{C}{\sqrt{\log(1/\widetilde{\epsilon})}}
\]
and
\[
\widetilde{\epsilon}
\le
C\Bigl(
\sqrt{\|\widehat{\theta}-\theta\|}
+
\epsilon
\Bigr)
\]
for some universal constant \(C>0\).

label: lm:polynomial-matching-bound

title: Proof
body_md:
First, the uniqueness of $p(x)$ is proved in Lemma 8.18 of \cite{diakonikolas2023algorithmic}. We focus on providing an upper bound on $\sup_{x \in [-C,C]}|p(x)|$ with explicit dependence on $m$.   First, let us define
\[
        q(y):=p(Cy), \qquad y\in[-1,1].
\]
It is easy to check \(q\) has degree at most \(m\), and for each \(0\leq t\leq m\), $ \int_{-C}^{C} p(x)x^t\,dx =  C^{t+1}\int_{-1}^{1} q(y)y^t\,dy$. 
Hence, $\int_{-1}^{1}q(y)y^t\,dy
        =
        b_t$, where $ b_t:=a_t C^{-t-1}$. 
Moreover, $\sup_{x\in[-C,C]} |p(x)|
        =
        \sup_{y\in[-1,1]} |q(y)|$.
Thus, it is enough to prove the desired bound for \(q\) on \([-1,1]\).

Next, let us write $q(x)$ as a Legendre polynomial expansion. A few standard properties of Legendre polynomials are provided in Lemma \ref{lm:legendre-polynomial}. 
Set $\phi_k(x):=\sqrt{\frac{2k+1}{2}}\,L_k(x)$ where $L_k(x)$ denotes the $k$th Legendre polynomial.
Then by Lemma \ref{lm:legendre-polynomial} (ii), we know \(\{\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_m\}\) is an orthonormal basis of the space of polynomials of degree at most \(m\) with respect to the inner product.
Therefore,
\[
        q(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\beta_k\phi_k(x),
        \qquad
        \beta_k=\int_{-1}^{1}q(x)\phi_k(x)\,dx.
\]
Write $\phi_k(x)=\sum_{t=0}^{k}\gamma_{k,t}x^t$.
Using the prescribed moments of \(q\), we obtain
\[
        \beta_k
        =
        \int_{-1}^{1}q(x)\phi_k(x)\,dx
        =
        \sum_{t=0}^{k}\gamma_{k,t}
        \int_{-1}^{1}q(x)x^t\,dx
        =
        \sum_{t=0}^{k}\gamma_{k,t}b_t.
\]
Next, we use the explicit formula of Legendre polynomial in Lemma \ref{lm:legendre-polynomial} (v). If \(0\leq t\leq k\) and \(k-t\) is even, then
\[
        |\gamma_{k,t}|
        =
        \sqrt{\frac{2k+1}{2}}\,
        2^{-k}
        \binom{k}{(k-t)/2}
        \binom{k+t}{k} = 
        \sqrt{\frac{2k+1}{2}}\,
        2^{-k}
        \binom{k}{(k-t)/2}
        \binom{k+t}{t}.
\]
If \(k-t\) is odd, then \(\gamma_{k,t}=0\).


Using the Legendre expansion of \(q\), we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
        \sup_{x\in[-1,1]} |q(x)|
        &\leq
        \sum_{k=0}^{m}|\beta_k|
        \sup_{x\in[-1,1]}|\phi_k(x)|  \overset{\text{Lemma }\ref{lm:legendre-polynomial} (iii) }\leq
        \sum_{k=0}^{m}
        \sum_{t=0}^{k}
        |\gamma_{k,t}|\,|b_t|\,
        \sqrt{\frac{2k+1}{2}}  \\
        &=
        \sum_{k=0}^{m}
        \sum_{\substack{0\leq t\leq k\\ k-t\ \mathrm{even}}}
        \frac{2k+1}{2}
        2^{-k}
        \binom{k}{(k-t)/2}
        \binom{k+t}{t}
        |b_t|\\
        & \overset{(a)} \leq  \sum_{k=0}^{m}
        \sum_{\substack{0\leq t\leq k\\ k-t\ \mathrm{even}}}
        \frac{2k+1}{2} \left(\frac{2ek}{t \vee 1 }\right)^t |b_t| \leq b_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{m} \left( 2k^2 \max_{1 \leq t \leq k}  \left(\frac{2ek}{t }\right)^t |b_t| \right)\\
        & \overset{(b)}\leq  b_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{m} 2k^2  \left(2e\right)^k \left(  \max_{1 \leq t \leq k}|b_t| \right) \leq 2m^2  \sum_{k=0}^{m} \left(2e\right)^k \left(  \max_{0 \leq t \leq k}|b_t| \right) \\
        & \overset{ (c) }\leq   2m^2  \sum_{k=0}^{m} \left(2e\right)^k \left(  \max_{0 \leq t \leq k}|a_t| C^{-t-1} \right)  \;,
\end{aligned}
\] where (a) is because $ 2^{-k}\binom{k}{(k-t)/2}\leq 1$ and 
$\binom{k+t}{t}
        \leq
        \left(\frac{e(k+t)}{t}\right)^t \leq \left(\frac{2ek}{t}\right)^t  $ when $t \geq 1$ and $\binom{k+t}{t} = 1$ when $t = 0$; (b) is because $\max_{1 \leq t \leq k}  \left(\frac{2ek}{t }\right)^t = (2e)^k$; (c) is because $b_t =a_t C^{-t-1}$.
